clue.text: Fans missing "dark beer" drinks

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so the quoted words are taken out of the longer word

blocks.note: fans of a team are its supporters
porter is a dark, heavy beer

explanation.surface: Supporters going without their stout at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove PORTER from the middle of SUPPORTERS and SUP + S remains. The quotation marks mark 'dark beer' as the thing to take away.
explanation.definitionFit: To sup is to sip or take liquid by mouth, so the verb form matches third-person drinks.

clue.text: Poet briefly working as comedian

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short and loses its final letter

blocks.note: John Keats, the poet this puzzle celebrates
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A poet with a day job doing stand-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Poet is the puzzle's theme, John Keats; clipping him and adding a word for working turns him into a silent-film star.
explanation.definitionFit: Buster Keaton was the deadpan star of silent film slapstick, famous for physical stunts.

clue.text: Good person briefly supporting a Lake Poet's most lofty expression

definitions.note: a noun phrase for a superlative adjective: the poetic word for 'most lofty'

indicators.note: cut short, so only a clipped form of the phrase is kept
in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this goes after what it holds up

blocks.note: taken as written
Lake Erie, one of North America's Great Lakes
a saint is a good person, abbreviated to St

explanation.surface: A saintly type propping up a Lake Poet as he reaches his highest note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake Poet' suggests Wordsworth or Coleridge, but Lake is ERIE on its own; the saint sits below A + ERIE in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Aery or airy means high up in the air, so its superlative is a lofty literary word for highest.

clue.text: Linklater's content to respond cheekily

blocks.note: surface reading: what the film director Richard Linklater feels or is happy with
setter's reading: the letters inside the name LinKLATer, which read backwards form a four-letter word for speak

explanation.surface: A film director's readiness to answer back.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer is an instruction. Take TALK and write it back and you get KLAT, which is what Linklater contains.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk back is an idiom for replying rudely or insolently to someone in authority.

clue.text: Win audience with small number that we hear might be Grecian

indicators.note: what we hear is what is spoken, so the spelling follows a sound

blocks.note: to get an audience is to get someone's ear
N is the abbreviation for number
Keats wrote Ode on a Grecian Urn

explanation.surface: Winning over an audience with a short Greek-sounding number.
explanation.walkthrough: Two routes to one word: EAR + N as a charade, and the Grecian URN from Keats's ode, which in a non-rhotic accent is said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to gain or secure something through effort, as one wins a prize or a reward.

clue.text: Novelist introducing last letters from Fanny Brawne in Time Out

definitions.note: the italics make it look like the London listings magazine

indicators.note: one who introduces goes first, so what follows comes after in the word
only the closing letter of each named word is wanted

blocks.note: Nevil Shute, author of A Town Like Alice
Fanny Brawne was Keats's fiancée

explanation.surface: A novelist featuring Keats's sweetheart's letters in a magazine piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Time Out is italicised as a magazine title; read plainly it means a rest, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut-eye is informal for sleep, and a nap is a break or time off from activity.

clue.text: Spurs game I must lampoon, ironically at first

indicators.note: to be game is to be willing to try anything, so the letters are ready to be rearranged
only the opening letter of each of the two words before it is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A fan vowing to mock Tottenham Hotspur's latest match, tongue in cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs reads as Tottenham Hotspur, the London football club, but it is the plural noun for incentives.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur is something that prompts action, the same as a stimulus, and both nouns are plural here.

clue.text: Mad? As mad as Fanny, perhaps

definitions.note: Fanny is an example of someone with this surname

indicators.note: something mad is crazy and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of the first two words; that the name also runs backwards through 'As mad as' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: Someone asked if they are crazy, answering that they are no madder than Fanny.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's other Fanny is Keats's Fanny Brawne, but this one is Fanny Adams, from the British phrase 'sweet Fanny Adams', meaning nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Adams was a real Victorian girl whose surname lives on in British slang, so she is one person bearing it.

clue.text: Setter blocked in by bus before lunchtime, cycling in Romanian city

indicators.note: something blocked in is hemmed in on all sides, so one piece sits inside another
placed in front, so the first part precedes the second
going round in a cycle, letters from the end come back round to the front

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter refers to himself as I
one o'clock, lunchtime, written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A setter stuck on a bus in a Romanian city before lunch, going round and round.
explanation.walkthrough: I inside BUS gives BIUS, then another I for one o'clock; cycling the last two letters of BIUSI round to the front gives the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibiu is a historic city in Transylvania, in central Romania, once European Capital of Culture.

clue.text: Clues note Psyche and suchlike, for starters

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
Psyche is the subject of Keats's Ode to Psyche

explanation.surface: Hints appearing in a note about Psyche and similar figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' sits between the two words that give letters; only Psyche and suchlike are tapped for their first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tips and clues are both hints that help someone reach an answer, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: "Bit of magic from outside right," said Mark Wright

indicators.note: one thing on the outside of another wraps around it

blocks.note: a tick is a mark made to show something is correct
R is the abbreviation for right
surface padding: completes the footballer's name, and 'Mark Wright' said aloud also suggests a tick, the mark for right

explanation.surface: Mark Wright, the England defender, praising a piece of skill from the outside right, a winger's position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside right' is an old football position, but here outside is the signal and right is R; Mark is not a name but a TICK that wraps it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trick is a conjuring feat, so it is one small piece of a magician's act.

clue.text: Writers putting Nightingale in Berkeley Square originally

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its start, so each opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the song title A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square, with Keats's Ode to a Nightingale in the background

explanation.surface: Authors bringing the nightingale of the old wartime song into a smart London square.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words from Nightingale onwards each give their first letter; Berkeley Square is a square in Mayfair, London.
explanation.definitionFit: A nib is the metal point of a pen, which does the writing, so nibs are writing tools.

clue.text: 13 week period of not quite mutual admiration finally shattered

indicators.note: not quite complete, so the word stops one letter short
only the last letter of the word is kept
something shattered is broken into bits that land in a new order

blocks.note: the word without its final letter
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A spell of shared admiration that ended in heartbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: The 13 looks like a reference to another clue, but it is part of the definition: a quarter of the year is thirteen weeks. Keats wrote To Autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn is one of four seasons, each lasting about three months or roughly thirteen weeks of the year.

clue.text: Retract Nancy's article, for instance

blocks.note: Nancy is a French city, and un is a French indefinite article
'say' introduces an example, like 'for instance'

explanation.surface: Demanding that Nancy withdraw an article she wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name, but it is a city in France, so her article is French.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsay something is to take back words already spoken, which is what retracting a statement means.

clue.text: Surveillance job with second coffee option provides clue to theme

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
coffee can be drunk in or ordered to take out

explanation.surface: Detectives on a stakeout, fetching their second coffee to go.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is a hint: read as an instruction, STAKE 'out' (rearranged) gives KEATS, the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A stakeout is a period of secret watching of a place or person, typically by police officers.

clue.text: Former postman, one now living abroad

blocks.note: ex means former
Postman Pat is a British children's TV character

explanation.surface: A retired postman who has moved overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: Postman Pat is a village postman in a long-running British children's TV series, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: An expat, short for expatriate, is someone who resides outside their native country.

clue.text: Free guitarist? Being given one for nothing gets rude rejection

indicators.note: being given one thing in place of another means a swap within the word

blocks.note: Paul Kossoff was lead guitarist of the 1970s rock band Free
one as the Roman numeral I
nothing looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A guitarist playing for free but earning only abuse.
explanation.walkthrough: Free is the band, not 'at no cost'. In KOSSOFF the O is swapped for I.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss-off is an informal, abrupt dismissal, especially the ending of a relationship.

clue.text: Suddenly gets angry, obscure fish appearing in reverse

blocks.note: someone who flips loses their temper
the ide is a little-known freshwater fish, much loved by setters

explanation.surface: Someone losing their temper over a strange fish swimming backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in reverse' looks like a reversal signal, but reverse is the definition, as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The flipside is the other face of a coin or record, which is the reverse side.

clue.text: Stick, ultimately one used in running slope

definitions.text: Stick, ultimately one used in running slope

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is used
put to use inside, so the pair goes within the other letters
running like dye or paint, the letters spread into a new order

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
one as the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skier's stick, ultimately something one uses when speeding down a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' does double duty: it gives its last letter to the wordplay and, with the rest of the clue, describes the answer as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A skier plants these long sticks in the snow for balance and push while descending a run.

clue.text: Male or female Lydians reimagined by poet

definitions.note: an adjective phrase for a first name that suits either sex

indicators.note: something reimagined by a poet is recast in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the Lydians were an ancient people of Asia Minor

explanation.surface: Ancient Lydians of either sex recast in verse by a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poet' wants to be the definition, and Vachel Lindsay was one, but the definition is 'Male or female': the name is given to boys and girls alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Lindsay is a given name borne by both men and women, like Leslie or Robin.

clue.text: Making new sort of punk, met Shaggy!

indicators.note: a new sort of something is a different version of it, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Meeting a new breed of punk and being amazed by his hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes Shaggy look like a name being called, but it is an adjective for messy hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaggy means rough and untidy in appearance, as unkempt hair or clothing is.

clue.text: Deny struggling with Melancholy and Indolence initially, performing as a handsome youth

indicators.note: a struggling thing thrashes about, so its letters are thrown out of order
initially means at the start, so opening letters are taken

blocks.note: the letters of the word
Keats wrote odes on Melancholy and on Indolence
an actor who is performing is on

explanation.surface: A depressed, lazy young man denying things while playing a pretty boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Only Melancholy and Indolence give letters; 'and' sits between them. Endymion is also Keats's long poem.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Endymion was a beautiful shepherd loved by the moon goddess Selene.

clue.text: Post from one we love

indicators.note: taken from a phrase, the letters are drawn out of the running words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Receiving a letter in the mail from a loved one.
explanation.walkthrough: Post looks like mail, but it is an upright pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel is the central pillar of a spiral stair or the post at the foot of a banister.

clue.text: Chain or whip, when not extremely penal

indicators.note: not at the extremes, so both outer letters are dropped

blocks.note: the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Choosing between chains or the lash, when punishment is not too severe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' makes chain and whip look like alternatives, but chain is the definition and whip is a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Catena is the Latin word for a chain, used in English for a connected series of things.

clue.text: Heads are those of Cupid and Psyche, inscribed "To Apollo"

indicators.note: points back to heads, so the leading letter of each following word is wanted

blocks.note: Keats's Ode to Psyche tells of Cupid and Psyche; Ode to Apollo is another early poem

explanation.surface: Sculpted heads of Cupid and Psyche bearing a dedication to Apollo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' does double duty: it is the definition and it tells you to take the head of each word after 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Capita is the Latin plural of caput, a head, as in the phrase per capita.

clue.text: Was happy with new pen?

indicators.note: happy as in happy-go-lucky, loose and carefree, so the letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: the letters of the word
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone delighted with the fountain pen they have just bought.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that pen is not a writing tool: a pen is a female swan.
explanation.definitionFit: Pen is the name for a female swan, just as a cob is the male bird.

clue.text: Part of 16 needing some bottle - and cheek!

blocks.note: the first part of 16's answer is kiss, and to kiss amorously is to canoodle
effrontery or nerve, as in having the brass to do something

explanation.walkthrough: 'some bottle' hints at a third sense: the narrow top of a bottle. Bottle is also British slang for courage, which fits the cheek sense too.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for kissing and cuddling, and a British noun for impudent nerve.

clue.text: Near neighbour of Douglas's, about to get some 6A

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man, and Peel is a town nearby on the island; the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: Someone living next door to Douglas, about to have a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas looks like a person, but it is the Isle of Man's capital; the neighbouring town Peel keeps its possessive S.
explanation.definitionFit: 6 across is shut-eye, informal for slumber, so any period of it is a spell of rest.

clue.text: Russian city cloaked in returning thick smog

indicators.note: something cloaked is wrapped up and concealed within what covers it
returning means going back, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A Russian city shrouded in heavy smog once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' reads as 'again' in the surface, but it turns the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Omsk is a large industrial city in south-western Siberia, on the Irtysh river.

clue.text: Bits of old verse periodically appearing as part of today's theme

indicators.note: happening at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Fragments of ancient poetry turning up as part of the day's topic.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme is Keats, whose best-known works are his odes, several of which appear in other clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's great lyrics, such as those to a Nightingale and on a Grecian Urn, are central to the puzzle.

clue.text: John recited with some force, that's clear

indicators.note: recited means spoken out, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: john is slang for a toilet, a loo
the CID, Criminal Investigation Department, is part of the British police force

explanation.surface: Keats's name read out forcefully so that it is plain.
explanation.walkthrough: John looks like Keats's first name, but it is the toilet; the CID is the detective branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucid means easy to understand, expressed plainly, which is one sense of the adjective clear.

clue.text: Playwright unknown in China?

blocks.note: Dennis Potter, writer of The Singing Detective
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A playwright who is unheard of in China.
explanation.walkthrough: China looks like the country, but with a small c it is porcelain; the question mark flags that it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: China is fine porcelain, which is one kind of ceramic ware made by a potter.
